text: quality summit 2006 11 We want to hear from other QE teams who manage their processes in facing similar challenges. quality summit 2006 13 Discussion Groups Table 23: ExtendScript ExtendScript is a complete, full-featured script engine which you can add to any application or plug-in. Its easy-to-use C++ interface connects you with a JavaScript engine that runs any script you feed into it. The core of the engine is currently being converted to use the Mozilla SpiderMonkey JavaScript engine, which is the reference implementation for the JavaScript specification. The integration of XML data into JavaScript according to the specification is supported. The ExtendScript Toolkit is a full-featured debugger and development environment that connects to any ExtendScript engine using the BridgeTalk communications protocol. For additional information or to sign up for the mailing list, please visit the ExtenScript twiki page: http://ctwiki.corp.adobe.com/bin/view/Main/ExtendScript. Discussion Points: • What kind

Table 24: BugHarvest The Bug Harvest method is a guided ad-hoc testing approach which is used by the InDesign QA team to get coverage quickly on new features and high risk changes. This method was used on various new features during InDesign CS2 with good results. It varies from a bug hunt by involving only the testers with relevant expertise, to cut down on ramp up time or duplicate bugs. Engineering involvement and QA communication in real time is also

the testers with relevant expertise, to cut down on ramp up time or duplicate bugs. Engineering involvement and QA communication in real time is also part of what has made the Bug Harvests work on the InDesign team. Generally, the tester who has ownership of the functional area will send out a general list of where to focus, so that everyone doesn’t start in the same place, but no specific testcases are used. This cuts down on the overhead for hosting. The main features of this concept that are new are: The outline should be loose, one or two words to define each “branch” or area of focus, which allows for tester creativity. The tests are run only when there are new changes or new features (so new fruit to be harvested), so this is a good method for high risk areas. The area is attacked by a cluster of testers, not one and not ALL of the testers, so this promotes teamwork without holding

ethod for high risk areas. The area is attacked by a cluster of testers, not one and not ALL of the testers, so this promotes teamwork without holding up the whole team. It gets new and different eyes on ALL of the areas. Less time and more flexible to adapt a tree to changes in the feature. No waiting if one tester has to go on PTO or leaves. When we lose one tester we don’t lose all of the knowledge for an area (more distributed info). We give the developers a batch of bugs to work on, and then time to fix them. Table B: Adobe Action Automation Tool The Action Automation Tool (AAT), created in-house at Adobe, provides a way for testers and engineers to quickly write automated tests which act upon InDesign or another client application at a user event level. The AAT allows for the rapi

nd engineers to quickly write automated tests which act upon InDesign or another client application at a user event level. The AAT allows for the rapid creation of event-driven tests. As UI often changes or is added to a developing application, the AAT is designed to handle the addition of new dialogs or palettes through an Acquisition process. Basically, a script is created which brings up the desired UI, then a description is generated. This description is read back into the tool and a set of actions is created to allow a user to automate the UI. If the UI changes, a support utility called a Transform can be created which is invoked to convert an older test case to the new state of the UI. Automation & Demos Host: Greg Christopher Hosts: Gregor Kaplan, Kevin Rice
Gregor Kaplan, Kevin Rice

quality summit 2006 16 The AAT is being used by testers of InDesign and InCopy in the US, India and Japan, and is also being used by CoolType. Prototypes and initial implementations have also been made for Acrobat and GoLive. AAT results are handled in one of two ways. The first is that a tester runs the scripts locally and after execution a results dialog is displayed. The other is through execution via a back end client-server farm system called Pulpo. Pulpo is our system for running thousands of tests daily and pushing results into a database. The results from the AAT are written both to a simple text log and to XML, which is what is parsed and entered into the DB. When a test is executed, an email is delivered to a list of people included in the Pulpo Job Ticket. This indicates success or failure and includes a link to a web site displaying results. The AAT exists as a set of plugins

ed in the Pulpo Job Ticket. This indicates success or failure and includes a link to a web site displaying results. The AAT exists as a set of plugins for the InDesign family of products and as a library for others. It is written in C++ and relies on client-product API’s to interact with the application. When it is used to test UI, the AAT collects information from the application to determine the location of controls or page items to generate UI events in the proper location. The AAT has been in use since late 2003, with a major effort to write automation in Fall 2005. The greatest limitation to the AAT is that it has historically been intimately tied into the Shuksan AKA InDesign code base. We are trying to take the basic concepts and utilities of the tool and port them to a more generic system which can be used by other applications. Another limitation is that not all UI changes can b

lities of the tool and port them to a more generic system which can be used by other applications. Another limitation is that not all UI changes can be automatically handled and sometimes things need to be massaged. Training has also proven to be a problem, but generally speaking the tool is easy to use and more flexible than canned solutions. The greatest advantage to the AAT is that it is resolution, language and platform independent. With very few exceptions, a script written on a Japanese Mac at 1024x768, will run on a French Windows system running at 1280x1024. The exception would be if the UI were significantly different between linguistic versions of the client application. A further advantage is that because the tool is in-house, we are able to fix and modify the tool rapidly. FMRs and bugs are generally fixed within a few weeks of being reported. quality summit 2006 17 Table C: Adobe Test Automation Framework (ATAF) ATAF provides a framework which enables UI-based test automation for product build validation, serial number validation, and component and integration testing. ATAF is used by Product teams, Core Tech QE staff, and Release Engineering teams. Supported products include Photoshop, Photoshop Elements, the Creative Suite, Production Studio, Illustrator, and Core Tech libraries (EPIC-Registration, CSI-Creative Suite Installer, AMC-Application Management Component, ESG (Engineering Solutions Group) platform build, Proximity-Dictionaries). ATAF was created in house using a commercial product (TestQuest) with customizations for Adobe. It was written through ATAF APIs based on C, and has been in use for 2+ years. The server runs on Windows, and supported clients include Windows, Macintosh, *nix, and handheld devices. Test resu

and has been in use for 2+ years. The server runs on Windows, and supported clients include Windows, Macintosh, *nix, and handheld devices. Test results are distributed via email notification, posted to a website, and are also available within the Matrix automated build system (BuildForge). ATAF also archives test data such as screen shots generated during the test run, ATAF and installer log files, and output from other test tools such as .jsx-based acceptance tests and product blueprints. This tool can be used by black box testers with support from the AMT (Application Management Technologies) QE Automation team. Advantages ATAF offers cross platform, multi-language support, does not require any hardware or software to be installed on the test systems, and closely approximates manual test execution (the automation is driven by simulating keyboard / mouse commands). quality summit 2006 18 Table D: BarCoded Forms Test Automation Framework Demo Testing the 2D barcode feature in Acrobat and LiveCycle requires a series of precise manual steps. As a core part of both Acrobat and Livecycle, this testing needs to be performed with all the major and dot releases in almost all locales and on most platforms. Testing involves filling in an Acrobat form (with various different UB rights), and on different OS platforms with various localized operating systems. The forms must then be printed, the printed forms scanned to create tif/pdf images, and then the images decoded to see that the encoding and decoding of the data is properly handled by the interplay of various libraries (including the 3rd party libraries). The fact that this is partly a hardware solution only adds to its complexity. The Automation Framework Tool actually streamlines the whole testing proce

e fact that this is partly a hardware solution only adds to its complexity. The Automation Framework Tool actually streamlines the whole testing process and removes the need for any manual tasks at all, saving thousands of hours of resource time and energy. The tool is designed to automate end-to-end testing of barcode encoder and decoder. Results are archived on a selected file server, and an email message with link is sent to the group, or to an individual tester if desired. Currently in use by the Barcoded Forms Server Team, the in-house tool’s architecture could be used by other groups as well. quality summit 2006 19 Table E: Basecamp Demo Basecamp is a server-based file comparison system. It is an in-house created tool written in Perl. Basecamp, in one form or another, has been used by various teams for over 6 years. In its present incarnation it has been in use for about 2.5 years, the latest release having been in production for 2 months. Suite Quality is using the system for testing InDesign, Illustrator and Acrobat; Acrobat QE uses Basecamp for testing Acrobat; and CoreTech for testing various components including AGMP and CoolType. There are systems located in Seattle, San Jose, and Noida. Basecamp can run on any platform that supports Perl (e.g., Windows, Mac OS X, and Linux). The current server release has been primarily tested under Red Hat Linux, while the client machines run Windows workstation. Certain Basecamp features and services provided by the clients will curr

ested under Red Hat Linux, while the client machines run Windows workstation. Certain Basecamp features and services provided by the clients will currently run only under Windows. The results are posted via a web-based UI. Advantages: • Basecamp provides a way to compare large numbers of files very quickly. • It allows testers to organize, manage, and report the results of those comparisons from build to build, or release to release. • It’s extensible and could potentially support any filetype for comparison. • It’s scalable. A single system can support many users and teams, the size and number of which are only limited by hardware. This substantially minimizes the cost of using Basecamp, especially for smaller teams. • Data format is XML based, making information sharing and integration with other testing tools easier. Limitations: • Someone still has to look at the results and with lar

ased, making information sharing and integration with other testing tools easier. Limitations: • Someone still has to look at the results and with large numbers of files, this can be time consuming if there are many mismatches. • Basecamp will only tell you whether two files matched or not; it’s up to the tester to decide whether the mismatch represents a bug. • False positives. The nature of an application under development is that it changes a lot and this can generate lots of mismatches that aren’t caused by bugs. quality summit 2006 21 Table G: DVA Unified Feature Database The Unified Feature Database (UDB) is a system used to track product features, their associated tasks, and the schedules of all DVA team members, including QE team members, something many teams had not done in the past. The Database was originally developed in-house for the Digital Video and Audio team, but has now expanded to most of the Creative Business Unit. It has been in use for about 6 months, so it is a relatively new system. The DVA team realized that there was a need to have all their features tracked under one tool. The two biggest advantages would be that the shared resources could be tracked together, and that cross-product dependencies could be scheduled. After investigating externally-created solutions like Microsoft Project, the teams decided that these solutions either lacked the ability to effectively track bo

tigating externally-created solutions like Microsoft Project, the teams decided that these solutions either lacked the ability to effectively track both Features and individual schedules, or they were prohibitively expensive. So the UDB was created as a way to do both. Filemaker was chosen as the environment to host this new system due to its low cost (thanks to our pre-existing site license), ease of use, the speed at which databases could be created and deployed, and its ability to run on both PC and Mac. Filemaker does have its disadvantages. First, there is an active-user limit of 250 on the database. Secondly, even though Filemaker can create schedules for each user in the database, it has limitations that prevent it from keeping those schedules up to date in the ‘live’ way that MS Project does. Therefore, it is up to each team to run a recalculation when they want to see the latest

schedules up to date in the ‘live’ way that MS Project does. Therefore, it is up to each team to run a recalculation when they want to see the latest schedule. Despite these limitations, however, teams have found it to be an extremely useful tool for tracking features and schedules. me actions are totally automated, like fetching or posting data from a system, while others involve collaborative human interaction. Each of these actions is a Quick Process Action Component (QPAC) that is used by a business analyst at process design time and executed by the workflow engine at runtime. It uses an action-based keywords strategy. A few important features of STAF: • STAF is independent of the complexities of SilkTest scripting. • Has an easy-to-understand Excel spreadsheet interface for creating test cases. • It has a Modular design for ease of expansion and maintenance. • It provides support for Automated Localization Testing. • STAF has multi machine execution capability and contains an exception handler for hang/crash test cases. STAF is written in 4Test (scripting language used by SilkTest) and has a modular design. It uses data table (Spreadsheet) for both input and verification, which reduces redunda

scripting language used by SilkTest) and has a modular design. It uses data table (Spreadsheet) for both input and verification, which reduces redundancy and duplication of effort in creating automated test scripts. It has been used extensively in automating AMT component/Suite GUI testing for over a year now. Results are reported in HTML format comprising the following data: Action Name, Expected Result, Actual Result, Pass/Fail. Usage of STAF has reduced test case automation time by over 50%. quality summit 2006 24 Table L: Central Test Font Repository - A New Resource for All Adobe Quality Engineers The central test font repository was implemented last year by Type QE and is a collection of fonts (both 3rd party and Adobe fonts) that have been legally blessed for testing use. Both Quality Engineers and Developers are encouraged to acquire the fonts that they need for testing Adobe applications from the repository and can benefit from the rich collection of fonts which has been assembled. The goal is to continue to add third party fonts as legal permission is acquired and enrich the set of available test fonts, but at present the repository already contains over 40,000 fonts from 15 different type foundries. Aside from having a centralized location for all Adobe employees to acquire fonts for testing, any Adobe employee can now search an online database and get help determini
